title: Holding debates kindly
hook: Sikhs discuss authorship and use of parts of it; the Rehat Maryada guides practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dasam Granth today: installed at two Takhts, recited in the daily prayers. Your line was read and honored. What did you take off the shelf and use? Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.

Two cousins at a wedding, plates of food in hand, have drifted into an argument about a book. One says every page of it is the Guru's own. The other says some parts may come from poets at the court. Voices rise a little. An aunt walks over, hands them both a cup of tea, and says, sit down, and say it again, slowly. That scene, in one form or another, is part of Sikh life with the Dasam Granth. Today isn't about who wins. It's about the tea.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE BOOK.` → `THE GURU'S OWN, OR THE COURT'S?` → `TODAY IS ABOUT THE TEA.`

segments.voice: Here is what Sikhs discuss. First, authorship. Some Sikhs hold that the whole Dasam Granth is the Tenth Guru's own writing. Others hold that some parts may come from the poets around him, and they weigh each composition on its own. Second, use. Which parts belong in public worship, and which are better left for study? Sincere Sikhs, scholars and Sikh bodies have come down in different places, and this lesson takes no side. Now notice what keeps daily life steady while the conversation goes on. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the shared code of conduct, names the compositions that are part of the daily prayers and the Amrit ceremony. That's the maryada at work. The word means a set way, a proper order, the limits that keep things in shape. So a Sikh can join the morning prayers with the sangat today without first settling every question about the book. The questions stay open; the practice keeps going. And the Gurus left words about how to talk. Guru Nanak, in a hymn on Ang 661 of the Guru Granth Sahib, says something like this: as long as we're in this world, we should listen to some and say some. Listen first is built right into it. Elsewhere Gurbani warns that speaking harshly makes the heart harsh too. Put those together and you get a way of holding a debate. Say what you think. Listen to what they think. Keep the shared practice in the middle where both of you can stand on it. And bring tea.
screen: `WHO WROTE IT? HOW IS IT USED?` · `A SHARED CODE KEEPS PRACTICE STEADY.` · `LISTEN TO SOME, SAY SOME.` · `THE PRACTICE IN THE MIDDLE.` · then, large: `DISAGREE KINDLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: disagree kindly once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one real disagreement you're in: at home, at work, online. Before you rehearse your side, rehearse theirs. Say to yourself, in their words, what they actually think, until it sounds fair. Then find one thing you both stand on. Then, and only then, your point, in a calm voice. If you pray, you can ask for a gentle tongue in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Holding debates kindly. Sikhs discuss who wrote parts of the Dasam Granth and how to use them, while the Rehat Maryada keeps the shared practice steady. Today's word.
Your line: disagree kindly. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's view back to them fairly before you give your own. Day one thousand two hundred forty-eight.
